newsitem.title: USA: U.S. spring wheat tour to see lack of uniformity.
newsitem.headline: U.S. spring wheat tour to see lack of uniformity.

text.p: Participants in this week's tour of U.S. spring wheat growing areas will likely see a lack of uniformity because of the hit-or-miss way the crop emerged earlier this spring, crop experts said.

The tour, which kicks off on Tuesday morning in Fargo, North Dakota, will also likely focus attention on the presence of diseases like scab, a fungus that can reduce yields and produce a toxic by-product called vomitoxin.
"For those who have been on the tour before, they're going to see more variability even across section lines," said Mel Maier, administrator of the North Dakota Wheat Commission.
Pat Berglund, director of the Northern Crops Institute, agreed.

"There's a pretty big variety across the state," Berglund said, referring to North Dakota, the top spring wheat state. "We're going to see a lush crop that may have some scab in the east. And we're probably going to see some areas that don't have a very dense population of wheat in the west," he said.

Maier explained that the spotty nature of this year's crop was a result of planting delays caused by the late snowmelt. But a subsequent early-summer drought also contributed to the patchwork emergence pattern, he said.

"Some of it didn't come up because of the drought after planting. Some of it came up sporadically -- if there was a low spot in the field, that came up, and where the seed didn't hit wet dirt it just lay there for two weeks. So that's why we have the lack of uniformity," Maier said.
In its July 11 crop report estimates based on July 1 conditions, the U.S. Agriculture Department shocked the grain trade by forecasting 1997 U.S. spring wheat production at only 569 million bushels.
That was down from the average industry estimate of 634 million bushels and was 17 percent below the actual 1996 production of 687.9 million bushels.

The tour, which comprises grain scientists, merchandisers, and statisticians, will take samples from wheat fields in Minnesota and the Dakotas. The numbers will be plugged into a standardized formula designed to calculate potential yields.

By the time the tour concludes on Thursday in Fargo, members will have come up with a potential yield estimate for the entire three-day trek, which will then be compared to last year's estimate and to USDA production estimates.
The USDA pegged this year's spring wheat yield at 30.4 bushels per acre, which would be sharply lower than actual 1996 U.S. spring wheat yield of 35.1 bushels per acre.
Last year's tour ended with an average potential spring wheat yield of 36.4 bushels per acre.
North Dakota harvested 313.5 million bushels of spring wheat in 1996, up from 221.4 million in 1995. But in its July report, USDA estimated this year's North Dakota crop at 212.5 million bushels.

"There seems to be a feeling that (the USDA estimate) for North Dakota is a little low, and I might subscribe to that theory if we don't have a bad scab problem," Maier said. "Given the development of this crop under decent conditions, I think we could see a little more wheat in North Dakota."
Plant pathologists said that the chance for scab to develop into a major threat has lessened in recent weeks as hot weather has created an inhospitable environment for the fungus.
But few people in the grain trade seem willing to write off the scab threat.

"There's some concern about scab," a Minnesota grain dealer said. "It's been really wet and humid. We really don't know yet about the extent of the damage but with these weather conditions, it's almost a given we'll have problems."
